By focusing on formate, a readily available and inexpensive C1 feedstock, USF sought to demonstrate a viable pathway that could be scaled for industrial applications. 4 The primary goals were to identify suitable enzyme candidates, characterize bacterial host strains, prototype the bioconversion pathway, engineer microorganisms, and develop a robust bioconversion process. Key accomplishments include: 1. Identification and Characterization of Enzyme Candidates and Host Strains (Months 1-12): Using bioinformatics tools and experimental assays, USF identified optimal enzymes for catalyzing each step of the ethylene glycol pathway. Concurrently, various bacterial strains were evaluated for their ability to withstand the industrial-relevant conditions, resulting in the selection of robust hosts for genetic engineering. 2. Pathway Prototyping and Microorganism Engineering (Months 13-35): Building on earlier findings, the team successfully prototyped the conversion pathway using both in vitro and in vivo approaches. This included the development of engineered strains with tailored genetic modifications to enhance pathway efficiency and stability. 3. Development of Bioconversion Process (Months 22-48): The engineered strains were extensively tested under varying conditions to optimize ethylene glycol production. The project culminated in a scalable bioconversion process that achieved 2.3 g/L ethylene glycol yield, surpassing the initial target of 1 g/L. The methodologies employed by USF have proven technically effective, showcasing the ability to rapidly iterate and optimize both biological and process engineering aspects. Economically, the project lays the groundwork for a cost-effective alternative to petrochemical routes, highlighting the potential for commercial viability. This project contributes significantly to understanding C1 utilization in industrial biotechnology, offering a promising avenue for the sustainable production of chemicals. Its success not only advances scientific and technical knowledge but also has the potential to influence future clean energy policies and practices, promoting a shift towards greener technologies. 5
